If a model contains dilated convolution and uses JIT trace to export to TorchScript Module, the exported module will run slower in C++ inference than in Python on CPU.
For an internal model the slow down is significant, where Python inference takes ~10s with OMP_NUM_THREADS=2, and C++ inference takes ~31s.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Use the following code to export a ResNet101 model with modified dilation:

import torch
from torchvision import models
import time

net = models.resnet101(pretrained=True).cpu()
# artificially create a dilation layer 
net.conv1.dilation=(3, 3)
net = net.eval()

# 4batch size
example = torch.rand(4, 3, 224, 224).cpu()

with torch.no_grad():
    traced_script_module = torch.jit.trace(net, example)

traced_script_module.save('traced_resnet101_dilation.pt')

Use the following code for Python inference profiling:

from __future__ import print_function

import os
import sys
import time
import torch

traced_script_module = torch.jit.load(sys.argv[1])
example = torch.rand(4, 3, 224, 224).cpu()

with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(5):
        start_ts = time.time()
        with torch.autograd.profiler.profile() as profile:
            traced_script_module(example)
        end_ts = time.time()
        print('inference took {:.2f}ms'.format((end_ts - start_ts) * 1000))

        profile.export_chrome_trace('profile_python_cpu.json')

There are separate implementations for the distributed data parallelism for CUDA and CPU tensors.
The CUDA one has evolved quite a bit and includes:

Dynamic bucketing of gradient tensors to reduce the number of reduction calls
Start reduction when a bucket is full (i.e. all gradients participating have been computed)
Handling of fp32 and fp16 gradients
Handling of multiple model copies across devices
Buffer broadcast

The CPU one has not evolved and does the following:

Wait for all gradients to be computed
Flatten all gradients into one big tensor
Allreduce
Unflatten

Ideally, we turn the CUDA approach into a device agnostic one, such that we can remove the CPU specific implementation. Parts of the CUDA approach are written in C++ (see #12852, #12954, #13496, #13607) and these can be made device agnostic as well. Both the bucketing and autograd hooks are now defined in Python land but can be turned into C++ code as well.
Separately, @mcarilli and team made really nice improvements to standard DDP in Apex. The ideal bucketing order is discovered dynamically such that it reflects the execution order instead of definition order, which can cause significant speedups if these orderings are mismatched (e.g. layers that are used last are defined first).
Goals:

Use the same DDP implementation regardless of backend
Enable use of DDP for models defined with the C++ frontend
Discover ideal bucketing order dynamically

Let's use this as a starting point for discussion.

🐛 Bug? Or misuse?:
Traced LSTM works as expected, but when saving it to disk and loading it again outputs NaN and incorrect values.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1 Install Pytorch 1.0.0 or 1.0.1.
2. Run  self-contained script:
import torch
from torch import nn

T = 10
F = 20
device = torch.device('cuda')

print('Generating data')
data = (torch.rand(1, T, F) * 0.1).to(device)

print('Loading model')
model = nn.LSTM(F, F, num_layers=1, batch_first=True, bidirectional=True, dropout=0)
model = model.eval().to(device)

print('Tracing model')
tmodel = torch.jit.trace(model, (data,))
tmodel.save('/tmp/test.pt')

print('Productionazing model')
pmodel = torch.jit.load('/tmp/test.pt', map_location=device)

print('Forwarding data')
with torch.no_grad():
    o1 = model(data)[0]
    o2 = tmodel(data)[0]
    o3 = pmodel(data)[0]

assert (o1 == o2).all()   # WORKS
assert (o2 == o3).all()   # FAILS
Expected behavior
The above example shows 3 different versions of the same model:

model: raw LSTM
tmodel: traced LSTM
pmodel: dumped and loaded tmodel

model and tmodel calculate the same output. On the contrary. pmodel outputs wrong values + NaNs.
Issue also sent to Pytorch Forums:
https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/wrong-results-when-jit-exporting-an-lstm-module/38869

import torch
import numpy as np

A = (torch.rand(10, 10, 10) > 0.9)
i, j, k = A.nonzero().t()

🚀 Feature

We should get rid of special inplace handling in Declarations.yaml and corresponding generated code.
Motivation
The inplace entry in Declarations.yaml is essentially a subset of our schema annotations, but the semantics aren't totally clear: does it mean "only the first parameter is an output and only the first parameter is modified?"  But we have examples that are not expressible in that form, e.g.:
func: rrelu_with_noise_(Tensor self, Tensor noise, Scalar lower=0.125, Scalar upper=0.3333333333333333, bool training=False, Generator? generator=None) -> Tensor
writes to both self and noise and only outputs self, but that is not expressible without schema annotations, but is perfectly expressible with schema annotations.
Essentially, names just becomes names and the schema tells you what the actual behavior is.  Of course we may want to enforce certain naming rules, but the point is that code gen behavior (outside of naming) is triggered based by the schema annotations, not by the name.
This came out of a discussion with @suo.  CC @cpuhrsch @zdevito.

Feature
A modification of nn.Sequential class that would infer some input parameters for containing modules. E.g. in_features for nn.Linear.
Motivation
Inferring shapes of subsequent layers require manual calculations. Sometimes it is not trivial; e.g. in conv layers with non-default padding / output_padding / stride. In this case one require to look into documentation page for exact formula. Of course, it is a consequence of a dynamic-graph paradigm. However in the case, when the order of layers is predefined, e.g. in nn.Sequential container, it seems possible and would be quite handy.
Proposal
My idea is to first of all, implement a method infer_output_shape in every class inherited from nn.Module, which would take an input shape and return an output shape. Also, I need a method (let's call it infer_init_params) that would take an input shape and return a dict with arguments of __init__, that are inferrable from this input shape (e.g. number of input channels of nn.Conv2d is inferrable from input shape).
After that, I would like to extend an nn.Sequential class. I would like it to accept not only a sequence of nn.Modules, but also a sequence of either nn.Modules, or tuples of class and dict of kwargs, e.g. not only, say, nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3), but also (nn.Conv2d, {in_channels=3, out_channels=32, kernel_size=3}). The modified nn.Sequential class would also require expected_input_shape argument. The modified nn.Sequential class then will initialize as following: for every tuple in a sequence it will infer params to initialize a corresponding module. If all the params required to initialize a module are either inferred, or provided in a dict of kwargs, it will deduce an output shape, and infer __init__ arguments for a next module.
A code example:
model = nn.Sequential(
    (nn.Linear, {out_features=500}),
    nn.ReLU(),
    (nn.Linear, {out_features=10}),
    expected_input_shape=(None,784)
)

Here, in nn.Sequential.__init__ method we instantiate a nn.Linear object with in_features=784 deduced from expected_input_shape and out_features=500 that is given. Then we use nn.Linear.infer_output_shape to deduce output shape (None, 500). Analogously, we use nn.ReLU.infer_output_shape to again deduce output shape (None, 500). After that, we use nn.Linear.infer_init_params to deduce {in_features=500} from the shape (None, 500) and instantiate the second nn.Linear object with in_features=500, out_features=10.
Does this look too clumsy? If not, I would like to make a PR.
